description: First and last visibility of a planet, a star, or the Moon from a place: the heliacal rising (morning_first, the first morning a body is seen again before sunrise after its conjunction with the Sun), the heliacal setting (evening_last), the evening_first and morning_last of Mercury, Venus, and the Moon (evening_first for the Moon is the new crescent), and by the arcus method the acronychal_rising and cosmical_setting at opposition. These are the events ancient records report, and the dates depend on the place. The default method is a physical visibility model (sky brightness in twilight and moonlight, atmospheric extinction, the eye's threshold; Schaefer's published formulas), and the Moon's crescent uses Yallop's q test. Each event comes with an earliest and a latest date, the same event under a clearer and a hazier sky, because the haze on a given morning is not known. method 'arcus' is the classical geometric rule and needs arcus_visionis, the Sun's depression in degrees when the body is on the horizon. With no kind given, every event the target has is returned. Dates are the next occurrence at or after the start date; years are astronomical (0 is 1 BCE, -599 is 600 BCE) and the Julian calendar is used before 15 October 1582. target is a planet (mercury to saturn), 'moon', or a catalog star name such as Sirius, Regulus, Aldebaran, Spica, Antares.

altitude_m.description: observer height above sea level in metres

arcus_visionis.description: for method 'arcus': the Sun's depression in degrees when the body is on the horizon

extinction.description: V-band extinction, magnitudes per air mass: 0.15 a clear mountain, 0.25 a clear sea-level sky (default), 0.35 and up hazy

kind.description: which event; omit for every event the target has

spread.description: half-width of the extinction range behind 'earliest' and 'latest' (default 0.05)

start_year.description: year to search from, astronomical (negative for BCE: -599 is 600 BCE)

target.description: planet in snake_case (mercury, venus, mars, jupiter, saturn), 'moon', or a star name (Sirius, Regulus, Spica ...)

name: heliacal
